confirmed: Read the entire markdown conversion and all six PDF pages, including references through p. 6. The source is the EPDE 2024 conference paper EPDE2024/1149, with the 5-6 September 2024 conference header; title and all three authors match the form (PDF p. 1 and page footers). No appendix or supplementary-material reference is stated in this document (PDF pp. 1-6).

No randomized assignment of people, teams, or condition order is reported. Section 2.1 states only that the class was divided into groups and which groups were permitted each aid; retaining design_class = other, assignment.randomized = not_stated, criterion 1 = unclear, and context_class = none avoids assuming either random or explicitly nonrandom assignment. has_randomized_people_study = false means no such study is established by this source (PDF pp. 2-3, section 2.1; full document pp. 1-6).

Twenty-eight postgraduate students taking Design Methods at the University of Strathclyde were asked to participate; there were three groups of six and two groups of five. Thus the study cannot meet the 50-person threshold, regardless of the unstated novelty-analysis people count; no randomized-person count is given (PDF p. 2, section 2.1).

The two ChatGPT groups each had six students, the Google group had six, and the two control groups each had five. Section 2.1 prints responses received as 12 for ChatGPT, 5 for Google, and 9 for control; these are not separately stated analyzed novelty-sample counts. The form correctly leaves arm-level randomized and analyzed novelty counts null (PDF pp. 2-3, section 2.1).

The task was to generate a kitchen product for an arthritis sufferer using 6-3-5 or 5-3-5 brainwriting. ChatGPT and Google were permitted after students felt they had exhausted their own ideas; Google is a web-search comparator, and the ChatGPT model/version is not stated. The method description gives a 5-minute timeframe but no total session duration (PDF p. 1, section 1; pp. 2-3, section 2.1).

Novelty was scored on generated concepts using the paired criteria attributed to Oman et al.; three coders were used, each concept was reviewed by two coders, and the third resolved disagreements. The paper reports team averages, supporting construct = novelty, scored_on_output = true, unit = team, question = with_ai, and criterion 3 = met (PDF p. 3, section 2.2; p. 4, Table 2).

Direct PDF text and table extraction confirm all five Table 2 Group Average values: ChatGPT group 1 = -2.33; ChatGPT group 2 = -3.89; Google group 3 = -2.89; control group 4 = -5.06; control group 5 = -4.33 (PDF p. 4, Table 2).

The paper explicitly says scores closer to 0 indicate higher novelty. The reported string and one-line finding reproduce the ChatGPT and control averages correctly; no pooled ChatGPT-versus-control effect, SD, SE, confidence interval, or inferential test is supplied for novelty (PDF p. 4, section 3.2/Table 2; complete results and conclusions on pp. 3-5).

This is one original classroom study with a feedback survey and concept coding, not a synthesis; synthesis counts and pooled-estimate fields are inapplicable. Other reported creativity/helpfulness ratings are self-reports, and the paper explicitly limits its output coding to novelty (PDF pp. 2-3, sections 2.1-2.2; pp. 3-4, sections 3.1-3.2).
summary: Random assignment is not reported, and only 28 students were invited, below the 50-person threshold. The conference version and novelty scores are correct, but the form should leave the novelty-analysis people count null, record five analyzed teams, and document the survey-only exclusions.
